solution:
**Pyruvic acid** (two molecules of it).

Explanation. The chapter states that the process of glycolysis occurs in the cytoplasm, and that "a molecule of glucose is oxidized step by step in this process and two molecules of each i.e. pyruvic acid, ATP, \(\text{NADH}_2\) and water are formed". So strictly the chapter lists four products of glycolysis, of which pyruvic acid is the carbon compound carried forward — the two pyruvic acid molecules are then converted into acetyl-CoA (releasing two \(\text{NADH}_2\) and two \(\text{CO}_2\)) in aerobic respiration, or into organic acids or alcohol by fermentation in anaerobic respiration.

**Pachytene.**

[Note: this chapter never names any sub-stage of prophase-I, so the expected word cannot be sourced from it.] Figure 2.8 'Meiosis Part-I' (p19) draws the five sub-stages of prophase-I and labels them only with the numerals 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5 under the single caption "Prophase- I (1-5)"; no name is printed for any of them. The prose says only that "in meiosis-I, recombination / crossing over occur between homologous chromosomes and thereafter those homologous chromosomes (Not sister chromatids) are divided into two groups and thus two haploid cells are formed" (p19), and that "during this cell division, crossing over occurs between the homologous chromosomes and thereby genetic recombination occurs. Due to this, all the four daughter cells are genetically different from parent cell and from each other too" (p20).

So what this chapter does establish is that genetic recombination happens during prophase of meiosis-I, between homologous chromosomes. The name of the particular sub-stage — pachytene, the third of the five — has to come from outside this chapter.

**Metaphase.**

Explanation. The chapter's description of metaphase (p18) states it in exactly these words: "Nuclear membrane completely disappears in metaphase. Chromosomes complete their condensation and become clearly visible along with their sister chromatids. All chromosomes are arranged parallel to equatorial plane (central plane) of the cell." It is also in metaphase that the spindle fibres — "special type of flexible protein fibers" — are formed between the centromere of each chromosome and both centrioles. This arrangement in one plane is what allows the sister chromatids to be pulled to opposite poles in the next phase, anaphase.

**Phospholipid.**

Explanation. The chapter states that fatty acids are absorbed and distributed everywhere within the body, and that from those fatty acids different cells produce various substances necessary to themselves — giving as its example "the molecules called as phospholipids which are essential for producing plasma membrane are formed from fatty acids" (p16). Fatty acids themselves come from the digestion of lipids, which the chapter defines as "the substances formed by specific chemical bond between fatty acids and alcohol". So the plasma membrane is built from a class of molecule that the body derives from the lipids in the diet.

**Anaerobic.**

Explanation. The chapter says that some higher plants, animals and aerobic microorganisms perform anaerobic respiration instead of aerobic respiration if there is a depletion in the oxygen level in the surrounding, and gives this exact case as its example: "our muscle cells also perform anaerobic respiration while performing the exercise. Due to this, less amount of energy is produced in our body and lactic acid accumulates due to which we feel tired" (p15). The chapter's anaerobic-respiration chart on the same page shows the route: glucose to glycolysis to pyruvic acid to fermentation to lactic acid, in erythrocytes and muscle cells.

Nutrition is the life process by which a living organism takes in food, obtains from it the nutrients it needs, and uses them to release energy and to build and maintain the body.

[Note: this chapter does not define the word 'nutrition'. It does not occur anywhere in the chapter body — only here in the exercise.] The definition above is assembled from what the chapter does say. It states that human and other animals consume fruits and vegetables while plants are autotrophs that prepare their own food; that "we consume all these various plant materials and obtain different nutrients like carbohydrates, fats, proteins, vitamins, minerals, etc." (p12); and that these nutrients are used both for energy production and for building the body's own substances — amino acids from digested protein are transported to every organ and cell, "from these amino acids, organs and cells produce various proteins necessary for themselves and the whole body" (p16).

Nutrients are the components of food that the body obtains from what it eats and needs for energy production, growth and proper functioning.

[Note: the chapter gives no formal one-sentence definition of 'nutrients'; it identifies them by listing them and saying what each does.] According to this chapter the nutrients are:

- **Carbohydrates** — obtained from milk, fruits, jaggary, cane sugar, vegetables, potatoes, sweet potatoes, sweetmeats and cereals such as wheat, maize, ragi, jowar, millet and rice; 4 Kcal of energy per gram; the excess is stored in liver and muscles as glycogen.
- **Proteins** — macromolecules formed by bonding together many amino acids; 4 Kcal per gram; those of animal origin are called 'first class' proteins.
- **Lipids (fats)** — formed by a specific chemical bond between fatty acids and alcohol; 9 KCal per gram; the excess is stored in adipose connective tissue.
- **Vitamins** — "a group of heterogeneous compounds of which, each is essential for proper operation of various processes in the body"; six main types A, B, C, D, E and K, of which A, D, E and K are fat-soluble and B and C water-soluble.
- **Minerals** — listed by the chapter among the nutrients obtained from plant materials.
- **Water** — "functioning of cells and thereby whole body disturbs even if there is a little loss of water from the body. Hence, water is an essential nutrient."
- **Fibers** — "also essential nutrients", even though we cannot digest them.

**Proteins are the macromolecules formed by bonding together many amino acids** (p16).

The chapter adds that proteins of animal origin are called 'first class' proteins, that we get 4 Kcal of energy per gram of proteins, and that amino acids obtained after the digestion of proteins are absorbed and transported via the blood to each organ and cell, where the organs and cells produce from them the various proteins they need — for example melanin and keratin in skin, ossein in bones, insulin and trypsin in the pancreas, actin and myosin in muscles, haemoglobin and antibodies in blood, hormones from the pituitary gland, and the various enzymes and cell-membrane proteins of cells (figure 2.4). In plants the necessary amino acids are made denovo from minerals, and the enzyme RUBISCO in plant chloroplasts is the most abundant protein found in nature.

Cellular respiration is the step-by-step oxidation of glucose inside the cells, by which the energy required for daily needs is obtained in the form of ATP.

The chapter puts it this way: "Carbohydrates of the food that we consume everyday are mainly utilized for production of energy required for daily need. This energy is obtained in the form of ATP. For this purpose, glucose, a type of carbohydrates is oxidized step by step in the cells. This is called as cellular respiration" (p13). It occurs by two methods — aerobic respiration, in which oxygen is involved, and anaerobic respiration, in which it is not. Respiration at the cellular level is distinguished in the chapter from respiration at the body level, where oxygen and carbon dioxide are exchanged between the body and the surroundings.

Aerobic respiration is the method of cellular respiration in which oxygen is involved and glucose is oxidised completely.

The chapter states that cellular respiration occurs by two methods, "aerobic respiration (oxygen is involved) and anaerobic respiration (oxygen is not involved)", and that "in aerobic respiration, glucose is oxidized in three steps" (p13). Those three steps are glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle) and the electron transfer chain reaction. Its outcome is given on p14: "a molecule of glucose is completely oxidized in aerobic respiration and molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are produced along with energy."

Glycolysis is the first step of cellular respiration, occurring in the cytoplasm, in which a molecule of glucose is oxidised step by step and two molecules each of pyruvic acid, ATP, \(\text{NADH}_2\) and water are formed (p13).

The chapter adds that glycolysis is common to both methods of cellular respiration — it is the first of the three steps of aerobic respiration, and one of the two steps of anaerobic respiration, the other being fermentation. It is also called the Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway (EMP pathway) after Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and Jacob Parnas, who discovered it through experiments on muscles (p15).

| Point of difference | Glycolysis | Tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle) |
|---|---|---|
| Site in the cell | Cytoplasm | Mitochondria |
| Substrate acted upon | One molecule of glucose | The acetyl part of acetyl-CoA (both molecules of acetyl-CoA enter the mitochondria) |
| Nature of the process | A step-by-step oxidation, not cyclic | "Cyclic chain of reactions" |
| Products stated by the chapter | Two molecules each of pyruvic acid, ATP, \(\text{NADH}_2\) and water | \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(\text{NADH}_2\), \(\text{FADH}_2\) |
| Extent of oxidation | Glucose is only partly oxidised, as far as pyruvic acid | The acetyl part is "completely oxidized" |
| Need for oxygen | Occurs in both aerobic and anaerobic respiration | Occurs only in aerobic respiration |
| Discovered by | Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof and Jacob Parnas — hence the EMP pathway | Sir Hans Krebs, awarded the Nobel Prize in 1953 |

Both descriptions are taken from pp13-15 of the chapter.

| Point of difference | Mitosis | Meiosis |
|---|---|---|
| Where it occurs | Somatic cells and stem cells of the body | Germ cells |
| Stages | Karyokinesis, completed through four steps — prophase, metaphase, anaphase, telophase — followed by cytokinesis | Two stages, meiosis-I and meiosis-II; meiosis-II "is just like mitosis" |
| Number of daughter cells | Two daughter cells | Four daughter cells |
| Chromosome number of the daughter cells | The chapter does not state a change; the cell doubles 2n to 4n before division and two cells result | Four haploid (n) daughter cells are formed from one diploid (2n) cell |
| Crossing over / recombination | The chapter describes none in mitosis | Crossing over occurs between homologous chromosomes in meiosis-I, "and thereby genetic recombination occurs" |
| Genetic make-up of daughter cells | Not stated by the chapter | "All the four daughter cells are genetically different from parent cell and from each other too" |
| What it is needed for | "Growth of the body ... restoration of emaciated body, wound healing, formation of blood cells, etc." | "Process of gamete production and spore formation occurs by meiosis" |

Drawn from pp17-20. Note that the chapter states the genetic outcome only for meiosis; it does not say in so many words that the daughter cells of mitosis are identical to the parent cell.

| Point of difference | Aerobic respiration | Anaerobic respiration |
|---|---|---|
| Oxygen | Oxygen is involved | Oxygen is not involved |
| Steps | Three steps — glycolysis, tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle), electron transfer chain reaction | Two steps — glycolysis and fermentation |
| Oxidation of glucose | Glucose is completely oxidised | "Glucose is incompletely oxidized" |
| Energy obtained | More energy | "Less amount of energy is obtained" |
| End products | \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), along with energy | Pyruvic acid is converted "into other organic acids or alcohol with the help of some enzymes" — lactic acid in erythrocytes and muscle cells, alcohol in yeast, and different products such as vinegar and vitamins in various microbes |
| Site | Glycolysis in the cytoplasm; the Krebs cycle and the electron transfer chain reaction in the mitochondria | Glycolysis in the cytoplasm; the chapter does not state where fermentation occurs |
| Examples given | The usual method in living organisms | Many bacteria, which cannot live in the presence of oxygen; seeds in soil submerged under water during germination; our muscle cells during exercise |

Drawn from pp13-15.

Because it is only with oxygen that the whole of the glucose molecule can be broken down to \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\).

The chapter divides cellular respiration into aerobic respiration, in which oxygen is involved, and anaerobic respiration, in which it is not, and it attaches the outcome to that division. In aerobic respiration glucose is oxidised in three steps — glycolysis, the tricarboxylic acid cycle and the electron transfer chain reaction — and "a molecule of glucose is completely oxidized in aerobic respiration and molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are produced along with energy" (p14). Without oxygen only the first of those steps can run: anaerobic respiration consists of glycolysis and fermentation, and there "glucose is incompletely oxidized and less amount of energy is obtained", the pyruvic acid being turned into other organic acids or alcohol instead of being oxidised further (p15). The two steps that finish the oxidation — the Krebs cycle and the electron transfer chain, both of which operate in the mitochondria — belong only to the aerobic route. Hence oxygen is necessary for complete oxidation of glucose.

[The chapter does not describe the chemical role oxygen itself plays in the electron transfer chain, so no mechanism beyond this is claimed here.]

Because although fibers cannot be digested, the body's handling of all the other food depends on them.

The chapter says so directly: "Along with all above mentioned nutrients, fibers are also essential nutrients. In fact, we cannot digest the fibers. However, they help in the digestion of other substances and egestion of undigested substances" (p17). So fibers are counted among the nutrients not because they yield energy or building material — unlike carbohydrates, proteins and lipids, for which the chapter gives energy values of 4, 4 and 9 Kcal per gram — but because they assist the digestion of the substances that do, and because they carry the undigested residue out of the body. The chapter adds that we obtain fibers from leafy vegetables, fruits and cereals.

Because everything a living body does that involves making new cells depends on it.

The chapter states: "Cell division is one of the very important properties of cells and living organisms. Due to this property only, a new organism is formed from existing one, a multicellular organism grows up and emaciated body can be restored" (p17). Those three consequences are the reason. It then attaches each of the two types of cell division to its own set of needs — mitosis, which occurs in somatic cells and stem cells, "is essential for growth of the body. Besides, it is necessary for restoration of emaciated body, wound healing, formation of blood cells, etc." (p19), while meiosis, which occurs in germ cells, is how gamete production and spore formation take place (p20). Without cell division there would be no growth, no repair of injury, no replacement of worn-out cells and no new individual of the species.

Because they switch to it when the oxygen around them runs short.

The chapter's reason is that anaerobic respiration is not confined to organisms that cannot tolerate oxygen: "Some higher plants, animals and aerobic microorganisms also perform anaerobic respiration instead of aerobic respiration if there is depletion in oxygen level in the surrounding" (p15). It gives two examples. Seeds perform anaerobic respiration if the soil is submerged under water during germination. And "our muscle cells also perform anaerobic respiration while performing the exercise. Due to this, less amount of energy is produced in our body and lactic acid accumulates due to which we feel tired" — which is also why the chapter's anaerobic chart shows lactic acid as the fermentation product of erythrocytes and muscle cells. So the switch is a response to a shortage of oxygen, and it is paid for in energy: glucose is then only incompletely oxidised.

Because the cycle is a cycle of tricarboxylic acids, and citric acid — an acid carrying three carboxyl groups — is the first of them to be formed when acetyl-CoA enters it.

[Note: this chapter does not mention citric acid at all.] What the chapter does give is the other two names and the reason for one of them. It calls the second step of aerobic respiration the "Tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle)" and describes it as a "cyclic chain of reactions" operating on acetyl-CoA in the mitochondria (p13); and it explains the name Krebs — "the cyclical reactions of tricarboxylic acid cycle were discovered by Sir Hans Krebs. Hence, this cyclical process is also called as Krebs cycle. He has been awarded the Nobel Prize in 1953 for this discovery" (p15). The link between the chapter's own word 'tricarboxylic' and the name 'citric acid cycle' is not made anywhere in the chapter and has to be supplied from outside it.

**Glycolysis**

**What it is and where it happens.** Glycolysis is the first step of cellular respiration. "Process of glycolysis occurs in cytoplasm" (p13) — not in the mitochondria, unlike the two steps that follow it in aerobic respiration.

**What happens in it.** "A molecule of glucose is oxidized step by step in this process and two molecules of each i.e. pyruvic acid, ATP, \(\text{NADH}_2\) and water are formed." So one glucose molecule yields:

| Product | Number of molecules |
|---|---|
| Pyruvic acid | 2 |
| ATP | 2 |
| \(\text{NADH}_2\) | 2 |
| Water | 2 |

**What happens to its product.** The route the pyruvic acid takes depends on whether oxygen is available.

- In **aerobic respiration**, the "molecules of pyruvic acid formed in this process are converted into molecules of Acetyl-Coenzyme-A. Two molecules of \(\text{NADH}_2\) and two molecules of \(\text{CO}_2\) are released during this process." The acetyl-CoA then enters the mitochondria for the tricarboxylic acid cycle.
- In **anaerobic respiration**, glycolysis is followed by fermentation instead: "pyruvic acid produced through glycolysis is converted into other organic acids or alcohol with the help of some enzymes" (p15) — lactic acid in erythrocytes and muscle cells, alcohol in yeast, and products such as vinegar and vitamins in various microbes.

Glycolysis is therefore common to both methods of cellular respiration; it is the one step that does not require oxygen.

**Who discovered it.** "Process of glycolysis was discovered by three scientists Gustav Embden, Otto Meyerhof, and Jacob Parnas along with their colleagues. For this purpose, they performed experiments on muscles. Hence, glycolysis is also called as Embden-Meyerhof-Parnas pathway (EMP pathway)" (p15).

The \(\text{NADH}_2\) formed here is not wasted: in aerobic respiration it goes on to the electron transfer chain reaction, where each \(\text{NADH}_2\) molecule gives 3 molecules of ATP (p14).

**Mitosis**

Mitosis is the cell division that occurs in the somatic cells and stem cells of the body. Before any type of cell division the cell first doubles the chromosome number present in its nucleus — "if chromosome number is 2n, it is doubled up to 4n" (p18).

Mitosis is completed through two main steps: **karyokinesis** (nuclear division) and **cytokinesis** (cytoplasmic division). Karyokinesis is itself completed through four steps, drawn in figure 2.6 of the chapter.

**A. Prophase.** Condensation of the basically thin, thread-like chromosomes starts, so they become short and thick and begin to appear along with their pairs of sister chromatids. The centrioles duplicate and each centriole moves to opposite poles of the cell. The nuclear membrane and the nucleolus start to disappear.

**B. Metaphase.** The nuclear membrane completely disappears. The chromosomes complete their condensation and become clearly visible along with their sister chromatids. All chromosomes are arranged parallel to the equatorial plane (central plane) of the cell. Special flexible protein fibers — the spindle fibers — are formed between the centromere of each chromosome and both centrioles.

**C. Anaphase.** The centromeres split, so the sister chromatids of each chromosome separate and are pulled apart in opposite directions with the help of the spindle fibers. The separated sister chromatids are called daughter chromosomes; while being pulled they "appear like bunch of bananas". In this way each set of chromosomes reaches one of the two opposite poles of the cell.

**D. Telophase.** The chromosomes that have reached the opposite poles start to decondense, so they again become thread-like, thin and invisible. A nuclear membrane is formed around each set of chromosomes at the poles, so two daughter nuclei are formed in the cell, and a nucleolus appears in each. The spindle fibers completely disappear.

**Cytokinesis** (figure 2.7). Karyokinesis is now complete and cytokinesis begins. The cytoplasm divides and two new cells — the daughter cells — are formed. "In this process, a notch is formed at the equatorial plane of the cell which deepens gradually and thereby two new cells are formed. However, in case of plant cells, instead of the notch, a cell plate is formed exactly along midline of the cell and thus cytokinesis is completed" (p19).

**Why it matters.** "Mitosis is essential for growth of the body. Besides, it is necessary for restoration of emaciated body, wound healing, formation of blood cells, etc."

The chapter's figure 2.10 shows these phases as they are actually seen in a slide of onion root tip.

[The diagrams the question asks for are figures 2.6 (Mitosis), 2.7 (Cytokinesis) and 2.10 (Phases of mitosis in onion root tip) on pp18-20 of the textbook; they are not reproduced here.]

[Note: this chapter does not name or describe the five stages of prophase-I. Figure 2.8 'Meiosis Part-I' (p19) draws them as five cells labelled only 1, 2, 3, 4 and 5, under the single caption "Prophase- I (1-5)". No text anywhere in the chapter discusses them individually, so an answer naming them cannot be grounded in this chapter.]

What the chapter does establish about prophase-I is the following.

- Meiosis occurs in germ cells and is completed through two stages, meiosis-I and meiosis-II (pp17, 19).
- Prophase-I passes through five sub-stages, shown as the five numbered drawings of figure 2.8. The drawings show the chromosomes progressively condensing from a thin thread-like state, coming together with their homologous partners, and the paired homologous chromosomes then becoming distinct and moving apart while remaining in contact.
- It is during meiosis-I that "recombination / crossing over occur between homologous chromosomes and thereafter those homologous chromosomes (Not sister chromatids) are divided into two groups and thus two haploid cells are formed" (p19).
- The consequence is given on p20: "during this cell division, crossing over occurs between the homologous chromosomes and thereby genetic recombination occurs. Due to this, all the four daughter cells are genetically different from parent cell and from each other too."

The names conventionally given to the five sub-stages — leptotene, zygotene, pachytene, diplotene and diakinesis, with crossing over occurring in the third — come from outside this chapter, and the chapter provides no description against which to explain them. A student answering this question from the textbook alone can describe only the sequence drawn in figure 2.8 and the recombination the prose attaches to meiosis-I.

The chapter answers this by showing that no life process works on its own — each one feeds the production of energy, and growth and development then draw on that energy and on cell division.

**All the systems work together, and they work for energy.** "Various organ-systems are continuously performing their functions in human body. Along with the various systems like digestive, respiratory, circulatory, excretory and control systems, different external and internal organs are performing their functions independently but through a complete co-ordination" (p12). Those systems need a continuous source of energy, and the chapter states plainly how each contributes: carbohydrates, fats and lipids are the main sources of that energy and it is harvested by the mitochondria present in each cell; oxygen as well as foodstuff is necessary; "all these i.e. food stuffs and oxygen are transported up to the cell via circulatory system"; and the whole is "coordinated by the control system of the body. i.e. each life process contributes in its own way in the process of energy production. Functioning of all these life processes also requires the energy."

So the contribution of each is:

| Life process | What it contributes |
|---|---|
| Nutrition / digestion | Supplies the carbohydrates, proteins, lipids, vitamins, minerals, water and fibers; digestion breaks proteins into amino acids and lipids into fatty acids |
| Respiration (body level) | Exchanges oxygen and carbon dioxide between the body and the surroundings |
| Circulation | Transports the food stuffs and the oxygen up to every cell, and carries amino acids to each organ and cell |
| Cellular respiration | Oxidises glucose step by step in the cells to release the energy, in the form of ATP — the "energy currency" of the cell |
| Excretion | Removes the waste materials produced in the body, such as the ammonia formed when excess amino acids are broken down |
| Control system | Co-ordinates all of the above |

**Growth and development themselves.** Energy alone is not growth. The materials absorbed are built into the body's own substances — from amino acids "organs and cells produce various proteins necessary for themselves and the whole body", such as ossein in bones, actin and myosin in muscles and haemoglobin in blood (p16), while phospholipids made from fatty acids build the plasma membrane of every new cell. And the increase in cell number comes from cell division: "due to this property only, a new organism is formed from existing one, a multicellular organism grows up and emaciated body can be restored" (p17), mitosis being "essential for growth of the body" and for wound healing and the formation of blood cells (p19).

Growth and development are therefore the joint result of all the life processes: nutrition supplies the raw material, respiration and circulation deliver oxygen and remove waste, cellular respiration releases the energy every one of these processes needs, and cell division turns the material and the energy into new cells and a larger body.

**The tricarboxylic acid cycle (Krebs cycle)**

[Note: the chapter prints no chemical equation for the Krebs cycle — there is no reaction written out anywhere in this chapter. What follows is the chapter's own account in words, together with figure 2.2.]

**Where it happens.** The Krebs cycle is the second of the three steps of aerobic respiration. "Both molecules of acetyl-CoA enter the mitochondria. Cyclic chain of reactions called as tricarboxylic acid cycle is operated on it in the mitochondria" (p13). Figure 2.2 'Mitochondria and Tri-carboxylic acid cycle' (p14) draws the TCA cycle in the mitochondrial matrix, inside the inner membrane, with pyruvic acid and fatty acids entering as acetyl-CoA.

**What enters it.** Acetyl-CoA. This comes from two sources according to the chapter:

- from carbohydrates — the two molecules of pyruvic acid formed in glycolysis are converted into acetyl-CoA, releasing two molecules of \(\text{NADH}_2\) and two of \(\text{CO}_2\);
- from lipids and proteins when carbohydrates are insufficient, "due to exceptional conditions like fasting and hunger" — lipids are converted into fatty acids and proteins into amino acids, and "fatty acids and amino acids are converted into acetyl-CoA and energy is obtained through complete oxidation of acetyl-CoA by the process of Krebs cycle in mitochondria" (p14).

**What happens in it.** "Acetyl part of acetyl-CoA is completely oxidized through this cyclical process and molecules \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\), \(\text{NADH}_2\), \(\text{FADH}_2\) are derived" (p13). Figure 2.2 shows the \(\text{CO}_2\) leaving and the NADH and \(\text{FADH}_2\) being produced at the cycle.

**What its products are used for.** The \(\text{NADH}_2\) and \(\text{FADH}_2\) do not stay as they are — they pass to the third step, the electron transfer chain reaction, which is also operated in mitochondria only. There "3 molecules of ATP are obtained from each \(\text{NADH}_2\) molecule and 2 molecules of ATP from each \(\text{FADH}_2\) molecule", and water molecules are formed besides the ATP (p14). This is how the energy released in the cycle is finally captured as ATP.

**Its name.** "The cyclical reactions of tricarboxylic acid cycle were discovered by Sir Hans Krebs. Hence, this cyclical process is also called as Krebs cycle. He has been awarded the Nobel Prize in 1953 for this discovery" (p15).

The overall outcome of the cycle together with the step that follows it is the chapter's summary of aerobic respiration: a molecule of glucose is completely oxidised, and \(\text{CO}_2\) and \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) are produced along with energy.

**How the energy is formed.** Carbohydrates, fats and proteins all reach the same place by different routes and are then oxidised by the same final pathway. Carbohydrates are broken down to glucose, which is oxidised by glycolysis in the cytoplasm to pyruvic acid; the pyruvic acid is converted to acetyl-CoA. When carbohydrates are insufficient — "due to exceptional conditions like fasting and hunger" — lipids and proteins are used instead: "in case of lipids, they are converted into fatty acids whereas proteins into amino acids. Fatty acids and amino acids are converted into acetyl-CoA and energy is obtained through complete oxidation of acetyl-CoA by the process of Krebs cycle in mitochondria" (p14). The acetyl-CoA from all three sources enters the Krebs cycle in the mitochondria, where it is completely oxidised to \(\text{CO}_2\), \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) and energy — the energy being captured as ATP through the electron transfer chain reaction, at 3 ATP per \(\text{NADH}_2\) and 2 ATP per \(\text{FADH}_2\).

**The corrected diagram.** The chapter prints the correct version of this very chart on p15, under the title "Process of energy production through aerobic respiration of carbohydrates, proteins and fats". It runs:

| Level (bottom to top) | Left column | Middle column | Right column |
|---|---|---|---|
| Food component | Lipids | Carbohydrates | Proteins |
| First product | Fatty acids | Glycolysis | Amino acids |
| Next | | Pyruvic acid | |
| Common intermediate | | Acetyl-CoA (the left and right columns feed into it) | |
| Final pathway | | Krebs Cycle | |
| End products | | \(\text{CO}_2\) + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) + Energy | |

**The corrections needed, box by box:**

| Box in the printed chart | Printed | Should be |
|---|---|---|
| Bottom row, left | Proteins | Lipids |
| Bottom row, middle | krebs cycle | Carbohydrates |
| Bottom row, right | Fats | Proteins |
| Second row, left | Lipid | Fatty acids |
| Second row, middle | Glycolysis | Glycolysis — already correct |
| Second row, right | Amino acids | Amino acids — already correct |
| Third row (blank) | — | Pyruvic acid |
| Fourth row | Acetyl Co-Enzyme A | Acetyl-CoA — already correct |
| Fifth row (blank) | — | Krebs cycle |
| Top row | Pyruvic Acid | \(\text{CO}_2\) + \(\text{H}_2\text{O}\) + Energy |

In short: the three food components in the bottom row have been shuffled, "krebs cycle" has been put at the bottom where the carbohydrate belongs, and "Pyruvic Acid" has been put at the top where the end products belong. Pyruvic acid in fact belongs immediately above glycolysis, and the Krebs cycle immediately above acetyl-CoA.
